title: I designed a dragon-hunting logic roguelike and built it with an AI as my development partner. Here’s how we split the work, and why it worked.
author: PsychoWynd
selftext:
(Commercial Self Promotion might also be in effect here)  
  
Wyrmdoku started with one idea: what if a “one per row, column and region” logic puzzle like Queens or Meowdoku wasn’t just a daily brain teaser, but the heart of a full roguelike? Today it’s in open testing on Android. You hunt dragons through caves, choose your path between merchants, campfires and cursed idols, build a run with relics, face a wyrm that wakes up the longer you take, and descend into the Deep as far as you dare. There’s a new daily lair for everyone each day and a weekly league. 🐉

The way I worked with Claude felt like running a small studio. I’m the designer and director: I came up with the mechanics, balanced the economy, decided what makes a cave fair but tense, playtested every change on my phone and turned my testers’ feedback into the next update. Claude is the engineer who can build at incredible speed: the puzzle generator, the Android app, Google Play leaderboards, cloud saves, a full English and Dutch version, and automated tests that checks every screen and the game's performance on older hardware.

That combination is what made it possible for one person to ship something this complete. I could try a design idea in the morning and play it that afternoon. When something wasn’t fun, I threw it out; when testers loved something, I doubled down. The AI never had to guess what the game should be as I tried to write prompts as complete as possible, so I never had to wait weeks to find out if an idea worked. The memory file was also of big help when working on the project.

I’d love your feedback, and I’m curious: how do you divide the work between you and your AI? Do you keep in charge or let your AI do all the thinking as well?
